title: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
summary: Prompt an LLM to rerank search results: yes/no and query-likelihood scores, PRP pairwise comparisons, RankGPT sliding windows, their call and token costs, position bias, and distilled rerankers.
outcomes: Explain how pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompts turn LLM outputs into a ranking and what each needs from the API
Compute LLM call counts for PRP-Allpair, PRP-Sliding-K and RankGPT sliding windows for a given N, w and s
Trace a back-to-front sliding window and predict which passages are guaranteed to reach the top
Estimate token cost and sequential latency for each method under a stated cost model
Diagnose position bias and malformed outputs and choose fixes such as swapping, self-consistency or distillation

lessons.title: Why use an LLM as the last-stage reranker

blocks.md:
A cross-encoder reranker reads the query and one passage together and outputs a relevance score. It is accurate, but it is trained on labeled pairs such as MS MARCO, and the notion of relevance it learned is frozen into its weights.

An **LLM reranker** reuses a general instruction-following model instead. You describe the task in a prompt, paste in the query and some candidates, and read the model's judgment from its output. No ranking-specific training is needed (the zero-shot setting), and you can change the criteria by editing the instruction.

The price is cost. An LLM call is far slower and more expensive than a cross-encoder forward pass, so LLM rerankers sit at the very end of a search pipeline and only see a short list. In the RankGPT and PRP papers the LLM reranks the BM25 top 100; production systems often cut that further with a cheaper reranker first.

blocks.title: Where an LLM reranker sits in a search pipeline

scenes.caption: The first stage scores every document cheaply (an inverted index or an ANN search) and keeps a candidate list.
A cross-encoder can cut the list further. It costs one small-model forward pass per candidate.
The LLM reranker sees only the short list that survives. Each LLM call reads hundreds or thousands of tokens, so the list length directly sets the bill.

blocks.md:
There are three ways to phrase the question to the LLM, and they are the subject of this course:

- **Pointwise**: show one passage, ask for a relevance judgment, sort by the resulting score.
- **Pairwise**: show two passages, ask which one is more relevant, combine many such comparisons.
- **Listwise**: show a window of passages, ask the model to output the whole ordering, for example `[2] > [3] > [1]`.

They differ in how hard each prompt is for the model, how many calls you need, and how many tokens each call reads.

To compare them we use one toy query with 8 candidates, D1 to D8, in their BM25 order. Each has a hidden relevance grade from 0 (not relevant) to 3 (perfect). The best passage, D5, sits at BM25 rank 5, and another grade-2 passage, D8, sits last. The model outputs in later lessons are hypothetical, chosen to illustrate each method; every count and score is computed from them by a script.

scenes.caption: Eight candidates arrive in BM25 order. The reranker cannot see the grades; we use them only to score the result.
The relevant passages (grade 1 or more) are scattered: D5 (grade 3) is at index 4 and D8 (grade 2) is at index 7, the very bottom.
The ideal order is D5, D3, D8, D1, D6, then the grade-0 passages. A good reranker must move D5 and D8 up past several irrelevant passages.

blocks.md: We score a ranking with nDCG@5, the metric family the papers report (they use nDCG@10 on 100 candidates). Each passage at position $i$ contributes gain $2^{g}-1$ divided by $\log_2(i+1)$, and the sum is divided by the same sum for the ideal order, so 1.0 is perfect. The BM25 order scores **0.465**.

An LLM reranker is a prompt plus an aggregation rule. Pointwise, pairwise and listwise differ in what one call sees (1, 2 or a window of passages) and therefore in how many calls a ranking needs and how hard each call is.

blocks.question: Why do LLM rerankers usually see only the top 20 to 100 candidates instead of the top 1000?
options: LLMs cannot read passages longer than 100 tokens
Each candidate costs LLM tokens and calls, so cost and latency grow with the list length
The first-stage retriever's lower ranks are always irrelevant
Listwise prompts only support exactly 20 identifiers
blocks.explain: Every candidate the LLM reads costs prompt tokens, and pairwise methods even need many calls per candidate. Recall beyond the cut is lost, which is why a good first stage (and sometimes a cheaper reranker) runs before the LLM.

lessons.title: Pointwise: yes/no relevance and query likelihood

blocks.md: The simplest prompt shows one passage at a time. In **relevance generation** (used in the HELM benchmark and compared in the RankGPT paper) the prompt is roughly: *Passage: ... Query: ... Does the passage answer the query? Answer Yes or No.* The model's probability of the token Yes becomes the score, and you sort the candidates by it. It is the same idea as monoT5's true token from the cross-encoder course, but with an instruction-following model that was never trained for ranking.

blocks.tex: s_i = \begin{cases} 1 + p(\text{Yes}) & \text{if the output is Yes} \\ 1 - p(\text{No}) & \text{if the output is No} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: Relevance-generation score as written in RankGPT (Appendix B.2) and PRP. With p(Yes) + p(No) = 1 this is a monotone function of p(Yes), so sorting by it is sorting by p(Yes).

blocks.md: Pointwise calls are independent, so all 8 run in parallel in one round. Below are the hypothetical p(Yes) values our model assigns, in BM25 order.

scenes.caption: One call per passage, 8 calls in total. Each bar is the model's p(Yes) for that passage alone.
Colored by the hidden grade: green marks grade 2 or 3, the accent color grade 1, grey grade 0. Mostly sensible: D5, D3, D8 are high and D7 is low.
But the scores are not calibrated across passages: D3 (grade 2) gets 0.83, above D5 (grade 3) at 0.79, and D4 (grade 0) gets 0.55, above D6 (grade 1) at 0.30.

blocks.prompt: Sort the candidates by p(Yes). Which passage lands at rank 1, and does the grade-0 D4 make the top 5?
blocks.reveal: The order is **D3, D5, D8, D1, D4, D2, D6, D7**. D3 beats D5 by 0.04, and D4 (0.55) takes rank 5 ahead of D6 (0.30), which is relevant. nDCG@5 rises from 0.465 (BM25) to **0.834**, a big gain, but the two calibration errors cost the rest.

blocks.md: The second pointwise family is **query likelihood**. UPR (Sachan et al., 2022) flips the direction: prompt the model with the passage and the instruction *Please write a question based on this passage*, then measure how likely the model is to produce the actual query. By Bayes' rule, with a uniform prior over the retrieved passages, ranking by $\log p(q \mid z)$ is ranking by $\log p(z \mid q)$. UPR used T0 (3B) and reranked the top 1000 passages from retrievers such as BM25 and Contriever.

blocks.caption: UPR score: the average log-probability of the query tokens, computed with teacher forcing in one forward pass (nothing is generated).

scenes.caption: For a 4-token query, the model reads each passage and scores every query token. Values are ln of hypothetical token probabilities (for example ln 0.21 = -1.56).
D3 is fine on most tokens but q3 gets -2.41: the passage does not support that word. Averaging over tokens turns this into one score per passage.
Means: D5 -0.96, D3 -1.41, D7 -2.76. Sorting by the mean gives D5 then D3 then D7. Note there is no Yes/No token: the query itself is the target.

blocks.md: Both pointwise methods need token log-probabilities. Many chat APIs only return generated text, which is why the RankGPT authors could not run them on GPT-4. And because each passage is scored alone, the score must be comparable across passages (calibrated), which the PRP paper argues LLMs are not trained to provide.

How well does it work? In the Setwise paper's controlled comparison (Flan-T5-large reranking the BM25 top 100 on TREC DL 2019), Yes/No relevance generation reached nDCG@10 0.654 and query likelihood 0.557, up from 0.506 for BM25, with only 100 LLM inferences and about 0.6 s per query. Pointwise is the cheapest and most parallel option, but not the most accurate.

blocks.question: Your API returns only generated text, no log-probabilities. Which pointwise method can you still run, and with what limitation?
options: Query likelihood, because it uses teacher forcing
Neither; pointwise prompts cannot work without fine-tuning
Yes/No generation, but you only get a binary label, so many passages tie and the ranking is coarse
Both, as long as you set temperature to 0
blocks.explain: Query likelihood needs the probability of the given query tokens, which a text-only API cannot provide. Yes/No still produces an answer, but without p(Yes) you only get two buckets, so passages inside a bucket keep their original order.

blocks.question: Two passages get p(Yes) = 0.83 and 0.79 from separate calls. Why might the lower one still be the better passage?
options: Each score is produced in isolation, so small differences reflect calibration noise rather than a real comparison
p(Yes) is always inversely related to relevance
Sorting requires scores to sum to 1
The second call used fewer tokens
blocks.explain: The model never saw the two passages side by side. Its probability depends on passage length, wording and prompt quirks, so a 0.04 gap is not a reliable comparison. Pairwise and listwise prompts address exactly this.

lessons.title: Pairwise ranking prompting: allpairs, sorting and sliding

blocks.md: Qin et al. (2023) argued that asking a moderate-sized LLM for a calibrated score, or for a full permutation, is too hard. **Pairwise Ranking Prompting (PRP)** asks a much easier question: given the query and two passages, which is more relevant? The paper's template is short:

blocks.caption: PRP prompt template (paper Appendix E). Only two answers are valid, so it works with text-only APIs (generation mode) or by comparing the log-likelihoods of the two answers (scoring mode).

blocks.md: LLMs are sensitive to the order of text in the prompt, so PRP asks **twice**, once as (d1, d2) and once swapped as (d2, d1). If both answers prefer the same passage, that passage wins the comparison. If they disagree, for example the model says Passage A both times, the result is a tie. So one comparison costs **2 LLM calls**.

blocks.title: One PRP comparison is two calls

scenes.caption: Compare D1 (grade 1) with D5 (grade 3). First call: D1 as Passage A, D5 as Passage B. The model answers Passage B.
Second call with the order swapped. The model answers Passage A, which is again D5. Both orders agree, so D5 wins this pair outright.
Now D3 versus D8, both grade 2. Our model has a position bias on close calls and answers Passage A, the first one shown.
Swapped, it again answers Passage A, now meaning D8. The two calls contradict each other, so PRP records a tie instead of trusting either answer.

blocks.md: **PRP-Allpair** compares every pair and gives each passage one point per win and half a point per tie. With $N$ passages there are $N(N-1)/2$ pairs, so $N(N-1)$ calls. For our 8 candidates: 28 pairs, **56 calls**. All of them are independent, so they can run in one parallel round.

blocks.caption: PRP-Allpair aggregation (Qin et al., Eq. 2). Ties in the final score fall back to the initial order.

blocks.title: PRP-Allpair: points won by row against column

scenes.caption: Cell (row, column) is the points the row passage earned against the column passage: 1 win, 0.5 tie, 0 loss. 28 pairs, each asked in both orders, fill the grid.
D5's row is all wins: 7 points, so it ranks first no matter where BM25 put it.
The 0.5 cells are the 5 conflicting pairs: D1 vs D6, D2 vs D4, D2 vs D7, D3 vs D8, D4 vs D7. In our toy every tie is between passages of equal grade.
Row sums: D5 7, D3 5.5, D8 5.5, D1 3.5, D6 3.5, D2 1, D4 1, D7 1. Sorting (ties by BM25 order) gives the ideal ranking, nDCG@5 = 1.000.

blocks.md: Allpair is robust but quadratic: for 100 candidates it needs 9,900 calls. PRP offers two cheaper variants. **PRP-Sorting** plugs the pairwise comparison into heapsort, $O(N \log N)$ comparisons. **PRP-Sliding-K** runs $K$ passes of bubble sort from the bottom of the list upward: compare adjacent passages and swap when the LLM consistently prefers the lower one. Each pass is $N-1$ comparisons, and because only the top $K$ positions usually matter, $K$ can be small (the paper uses $K=10$).

blocks.title: PRP-Sliding: the first bubble pass, bottom to top

scenes.caption: Start from the BM25 order and compare the bottom pair, positions 6 and 7 (D7 above D8). The model prefers D8 in both orders, so they swap.
D8 moved up one. Compare D6 with D8: D8 wins again and keeps climbing.
D5 versus D8: D5 is better, so no swap. D8 stops here, and now the carried passage is D5.
D4 versus D5: swap. The pass now carries the best passage it has seen so far upward.
D3 versus D5: swap. Then D2 versus D5 and D1 versus D5 also swap.
After 7 comparisons (14 calls) the single best passage, D5, is guaranteed to be at the top, like one pass of bubble sort. nDCG@5 = 0.796.
Pass 2 (14 more calls) lifts D3 to position 1 and D8 to position 4. nDCG@5 = 0.941.
Pass 3 (42 calls in total) fixes the top 3: D5, D3, D8. D2 still sits above D6 lower down, which nDCG@5 notices only slightly: 0.965.

blocks.prompt: In the first pass, why did D8 stop at position 5 instead of reaching the top?
blocks.reveal: A bubble pass carries upward the best passage it has met so far. When D8 met D5, D5 won, so the pass continued with D5 and left D8 behind. That is why **K passes guarantee only the top K positions**: pass 1 places the best passage, pass 2 the second best, and so on (assuming consistent comparisons).

blocks.md: Note on counting: a pass over $N$ passages has $N-1$ comparisons. Implementations such as llm-rankers skip the already-settled top positions, so 3 passes over 8 passages cost at most 7 + 6 + 5 = 18 comparisons (36 calls) instead of 21 (42 calls); llm-rankers also skips unchanged pairs at the bottom, and on our toy it makes 17. We use the simple full-pass count, matching the paper's description. Sliding passes are sequential: each comparison depends on the previous swap, so only the two calls inside a comparison can run in parallel.

Pairwise preferences are not guaranteed to be transitive: the model can prefer A over B, B over C and C over A. Allpair just counts wins and copes; sorting algorithms assume a consistent comparator, so their output can depend on which pairs they happened to ask. The PRP paper reports robust results anyway but flags this as an open issue.

On TREC DL 2019, PRP with FLAN-UL2 (20B) reached nDCG@10 72.42 (Allpair) and 72.65 (Sliding-10), close to GPT-4 listwise reranking (75.59) with a far smaller open model. Only about 0.02% of its generations failed the expected format.

blocks.question: You rerank N = 20 candidates with PRP-Allpair, asking each pair in both orders. How many LLM calls is that?
blocks.explain: There are 20 x 19 / 2 = 190 pairs, and each is asked twice (original and swapped order), so 380 calls. For N = 100 the same formula gives 9,900.

blocks.question: A colleague runs PRP-Sliding with K = 1 and evaluates with nDCG@10. What should they expect?
options: The top 10 are fully sorted after one pass
The best passage reaches rank 1, but ranks 2 to 10 are mostly still in the initial order
Nothing changes, because one pass only compares the last pair
The ranking is reversed
blocks.explain: One backward pass carries only the best passage to the top. In the PRP appendix, Sliding with 1 backward pass already gives the same nDCG@1 as 10 passes (78.29 on DL 2019) but much lower nDCG@10 (57.58 versus 72.65).

lessons.title: Listwise permutation generation with sliding windows

blocks.md: RankGPT (Sun et al., 2023) gives the model many passages at once. Each passage gets an identifier, `[1]`, `[2]`, and so on, and the model is asked to output the identifiers in descending relevance, such as `[2] > [3] > [1] > [4]`. This **permutation generation** needs no log-probabilities, so it works with chat APIs, and the model can compare passages directly against each other.

blocks.code:
system: You are RankGPT, an intelligent assistant that can rank passages
        based on their relevancy to the query.
user:   I will provide you with 4 passages, each indicated by number
        identifier []. Rank the passages based on their relevance to
        query: {query}.
assistant: Okay, please provide the passages.
user:   [1] {passage 1, truncated to 300 words}
assistant: Received passage [1].
...     (one user/assistant turn per passage)
user:   Search Query: {query}. Rank the 4 passages above based on their
        relevance to the search query. ... The output format should be
        [] > [], e.g., [1] > [2]. Only response the ranking results,
        do not say any word or explain.
blocks.caption: Abridged from rank_gpt.py in the RankGPT repository (wording kept, including its typo). Each passage is its own chat turn.

blocks.md: A prompt cannot hold 100 passages comfortably, so RankGPT uses a **sliding window** with window size $w$ and step $s$. It starts at the **bottom** of the list: rerank positions $M-w+1$ to $M$, then move the window up by $s$ and rerank again, until the window reaches the top. Consecutive windows overlap by $w-s$ passages, which carry the best passages found so far upward. The paper uses $w = 20$, $s = 10$ on the BM25 top 100; its Figure 3 illustrates exactly our toy setting, 8 passages with $w = 4$, $s = 2$.

blocks.title: RankGPT sliding window: w = 4, s = 2, back to front

scenes.caption: Call 1 reranks the bottom window, indices 4 to 7: D5, D6, D7, D8. The model outputs [1] > [4] > [2] > [3].
The window is rewritten in place: D5, D8, D6, D7. The two best passages of this window now sit at its top, inside the overlap with the next window.
Call 2: slide up by 2 to indices 2 to 5: D3, D4, D5, D8. The overlap brought D5 and D8 along.
Output: D5, D3, D8, D4. D5 keeps climbing; D8 drops to index 4, because only the top 2 of each window travel on.
Call 3: indices 0 to 3: D1, D2, D5, D3. This window starts at index 0, so the pass ends after it.
Final after 3 calls: D5, D3, D1, D2, D8, D4, D6, D7. The top 2 are right; D8 is stuck at index 4 behind D1 and D2. nDCG@5 = 0.941.
A second pass (3 more calls) frees D8: D5, D3, D8, D1, D6, D2, D4, D7, the ideal order, nDCG@5 = 1.000. RankGPT itself runs one pass by default.

blocks.md: The window count follows from the loop in `rank_gpt.py`: window starts are $M-w, M-w-s, \dots$ while the start is not negative, so a pass makes $\lfloor (M-w)/s \rfloor + 1$ calls (if $s$ does not divide $M-w$, the last window stops short and the first few positions are never reranked). For our toy that is $(8-4)/2+1 = 3$. For the paper's setting, $(100-20)/10+1 = 9$ windows; the paper's cost appendix reports 10 requests per query (one more than the code makes; the paper does not explain the gap) and roughly 11 s per query for gpt-3.5-turbo (about 1.1 s per call).

blocks.prompt: Why does RankGPT slide from the bottom of the list to the top, not from the top down?
blocks.reveal: A relevant passage near the bottom must be able to reach the top in a single pass. Moving back to front, each window hands its best passages to the next window above, so the best $w-s$ passages anywhere in the list end up in the top window. A top-down pass carries the weakest passages **down** and lets a good passage near the bottom rise only within the last window it sits in; the PRP appendix shows the same effect for bubble sort, where 1 forward pass gave DL 2019 nDCG@10 54.10 versus 57.58 for 1 backward pass.

blocks.md: One back-to-front pass with window w and step s guarantees, for a consistent model, that the best w - s passages reach the top. Everything below that is only partially sorted. That is why the step is smaller than the window: the overlap is the conveyor belt.

The model's output is free text, so it must be parsed defensively. The RankGPT paper (Appendix F) counted failures on 97 TREC queries: gpt-3.5-turbo produced 14 duplicate identifiers and 153 missing ones, text-davinci-003 missed 280, and GPT-4 missed only 1. Models also sometimes refuse, for example by saying none of the passages is relevant. The reference parser keeps digits, drops duplicates and out-of-range ids, and appends missing passages in their original order.

blocks.title: Parsing a messy permutation (RankGPT receive_permutation)

scenes.caption: The window holds D3, D4, D5, D8. The model answered with a repeated id, an id out of range, and no mention of [2].
Every non-digit becomes a space, so the brackets and > signs disappear.
Convert to 0-based indices.
Keep the first occurrence of each valid index: the duplicate 2 and the out-of-range 8 are dropped.
Index 1 (D4) was never mentioned, so it is appended at the end in its original order.
Final window order: D5, D3, D8, D4. Parsing never fails, but every repair silently falls back to the input order, which is one reason listwise results depend on the initial ranking.

blocks.question: RankGPT reranks the BM25 top 100 with w = 20 and s = 10, one pass. The 3rd most relevant passage overall sits at BM25 rank 95. If the model ranks every window perfectly, where does it end up?
options: Rank 3
Somewhere in ranks 81 to 100, because windows only reorder locally
Rank 11, the top of the second window
It is dropped from the list
blocks.explain: In every window it enters it is among the top 10 (only 2 passages anywhere beat it), so it is always carried into the next window. The 2 better passages ride up the same way, and the last window (ranks 1 to 20) sorts them exactly: rank 3. A passage outside the overall top w - s = 10 has no such guarantee.

blocks.question: Which change most directly reduces the number of listwise calls for 100 candidates?
options: Shrinking the window from 20 to 10 at the same step of 10
Raising the step from 10 to 15 with w = 20 (overlap 5)
Running a second pass
Adding more few-shot examples
blocks.explain: Calls per pass are floor((M - w)/s) + 1. With s = 15: floor(80/15) + 1 = 6 instead of 9. The cost is a smaller overlap (only the best 5 passages are carried along), and since 15 does not divide 80, the last window covers ranks 6 to 25 and ranks 1 to 5 are never reranked. Shrinking w to 10 with s = 10 removes the overlap entirely, so passages could no longer travel between windows.

lessons.title: Cost in LLM calls, tokens and latency

blocks.md: Now put the methods side by side on the toy list. We count three costs: **LLM calls**, **tokens** (input and output, since APIs bill both and output tokens are generated one at a time), and **sequential rounds**, the number of calls that must wait for an earlier result (this sets latency when calls can run in parallel).

Cost model (stated assumptions, not measurements): query 10 tokens, every passage truncated to 100 tokens. Pointwise and pairwise prompts add 30 tokens of instructions, listwise adds 60 plus 5 tokens per passage for identifiers and turn wrappers. Outputs: 1 token for Yes or No, 2 for Passage A, 3 per identifier in a permutation. One pointwise call reads 30 + 10 + 100 = 140 tokens; one pairwise call reads 240; one listwise window of 4 reads 60 + 10 + 4 x 105 = 490.

scenes.caption: LLM calls. Allpair needs 8 x 7 = 56. Each sliding pass needs 7 comparisons x 2 orders = 14. Listwise needs 3 windows, setwise 4 calls (3, 3, 3, then 2 passages, as in llm-rankers).
Input tokens. Allpair reads every passage 14 times (56 calls x 240 = 13,440). Listwise reads each passage about 1.5 times (1,470) because windows overlap by half.
Output tokens. Small for everyone here, but listwise is the only method whose output grows with the window: 12 tokens per window, or about 60 per 20-passage window.
Sequential rounds. Pointwise and Allpair calls are independent (1 round). Sliding passes and windows depend on the previous step, so they serialize: 7 rounds per bubble pass, 3 for listwise.
Quality on the toy (nDCG@5): Allpair 1.000, Sliding K=3 0.965, Listwise 1 pass 0.941 (equal to Sliding K=2 at 3 calls instead of 28), Pointwise 0.834, Setwise 1 pass 0.815, Sliding K=1 0.796.

blocks.md: **Setwise prompting** (Zhuang et al., 2024) sits between pairwise and listwise. It shows $c$ passages labeled A, B, C and asks only *which one is most relevant*, so the answer is a single label whose probability can be read from the logits. Plugged into bubble sort, one call moves the winner up $c-1$ positions instead of 1, so a pass over our 8 passages takes 4 calls with $c = 3$ instead of 7 comparisons. On our toy one pass also lifts D5 to the top, but because the winner swaps places with the window's first passage, the rest ends in a different order: D5, D1, D3, D2, D4, D8, D7, D6 (nDCG@5 0.815).

blocks.title: How call counts grow with the number of candidates N

scenes.caption: Log-log scale. At N = 100: pointwise 100 calls, Allpair 9,900, Sliding-10 1,980, listwise (w 20, s 10) 9. Quadratic Allpair is the steep line.
Fewer passes cut Sliding linearly: K = 2 needs 396 calls at N = 100, but only the top 2 positions are guaranteed.

Listwise with a small window and step (w 4, s 2, the setting the Setwise paper used for 512-token Flan-T5) needs 49 calls per pass at N = 100. Fewer calls is not free: each listwise call reads w passages.

blocks.md:
Measured numbers agree with the counting. The Setwise paper ran every method with Flan-T5-large on the BM25 top 100 (TREC DL 2019; the sorting methods stop once the top 10 is found):

- Pointwise Yes/No: 100 inferences, 16.1K prompt tokens, 0.6 s, nDCG@10 0.654
- Listwise generation (w 4, s 2, 5 repeats): 245 inferences, 119.1K tokens, 54.2 s, 0.561
- Pairwise Allpair: 9,900 inferences, 3.01M tokens, 109.6 s, 0.666
- Pairwise bubble sort: 844.2 inferences, 381.4K tokens, 58.3 s, 0.636
- Setwise heapsort (c 3): 125.4 inferences, 40.5K tokens, 8.0 s, 0.670
- Setwise bubble sort: 460.5 inferences, 147.8K tokens, 29.1 s, 0.678

blocks.title: Measured cost per query (Setwise paper, Flan-T5-large, DL19)

scenes.caption: Average LLM inferences per query. Allpair's 9,900 dwarfs everything; note listwise needed 245 because of the small window and 5 repeats.
Average prompt tokens per query, in thousands. Allpair reads about 3 million tokens per query.
Average latency in seconds on one GPU. Allpair is batched, yet still slowest; listwise generation is slow because it decodes long permutations token by token.
nDCG@10 (BM25 alone: 0.506). The accuracy spread is small compared with the 100x spread in cost, which is the main argument for setwise and for cheap pointwise baselines.

blocks.md: With commercial APIs, cascades cut the bill. RankGPT used GPT-4 only on the top 30 after a gpt-3.5-turbo pass on BEIR; its appendix measured on TREC that this costs about USD 0.098 of GPT-4 per query versus USD 0.596 for GPT-4 on the full top 100 (2023 prices).

blocks.question: Your latency budget is tight but you can run many LLM calls in parallel. Which method has the fewest sequential rounds for 100 candidates?
options: PRP-Sliding-10
Listwise with w 20, s 10
Setwise bubble sort
PRP-Allpair
blocks.explain: All 9,900 Allpair calls are independent, so with enough parallel capacity they finish in one round, the same as pointwise. Sliding, listwise and setwise sorting are chains of dependent calls. Allpair is still the most expensive in total compute and tokens.

blocks.question: Listwise reranking of 100 passages needs only 9 calls, yet a cost-conscious team still finds it expensive. What is the most likely reason?
options: Each call reads 20 passages, and windows overlap, so each passage is read about twice; output permutations are also long and decoded token by token
Listwise calls cannot be cached
The API charges per identifier
Each call must be repeated 10 times for stability
blocks.explain: Call count hides call size. A 20-passage window is thousands of input tokens, the 50% overlap reads most passages twice, and generating a 20-identifier permutation is many sequential decode steps.

lessons.title: Position bias, robustness and distilled rerankers

blocks.md: LLM rankers are sensitive to where things appear in the prompt. In listwise prompts, models tend to use the middle of a long context less well, and failed or partial outputs fall back to the input order. So the **initial order** leaks into the result. RankGPT's own ablation (gpt-3.5-turbo, TREC DL 2019) shows how strong this is.

blocks.title: Effect of the initial order (TREC DL 2019, nDCG@10)

scenes.caption: RankGPT with gpt-3.5-turbo reaches 65.80 when the window sees passages in BM25 order.
Shuffle the input and it collapses to 25.17; reverse it and it gets 32.77, worse than BM25 alone (50.58). One back-to-front pass cannot undo a bad starting order.
PRP-Allpair (FLAN-UL2) asks every pair in both orders, so the input order barely matters: 72.42 versus 72.40.

blocks.md:
Three practical fixes follow from the mechanisms you have seen:

1. **Swap and agree** (PRP): ask both orders, treat disagreement as a tie. It doubles calls but cancels first-position bias.
2. **Permutation self-consistency** (Tang et al., 2024): shuffle the list several times, rank each shuffle, and aggregate into the central ranking with the smallest total Kendall tau distance (the number of passage pairs two rankings order differently) to all outputs. The authors report gains of up to 7 to 18% for GPT-3.5 across their sorting and reranking tasks.
3. **Feed a good initial order**: rerank the output of a strong first stage or a cross-encoder, so whatever leaks through is already decent.

Do not read a single listwise call as ground truth. RankGPT measured that even GPT-4 does not always produce the same ranking for the same passages in two overlapping windows (rank-biased overlap below 1). Run consistency checks before trusting fine distinctions, and never use LLM ranking for decisions with social impact without auditing for bias, as the RankGPT authors themselves warn.

Cost and instability motivate **distillation**: use a large LLM as the teacher, record its rankings, and train a small model to imitate them. RankGPT did this first: 10K MS MARCO queries, 20 BM25 candidates each, ranked by ChatGPT, used as targets for a RankNet pairwise loss. The resulting DeBERTa-large cross-encoder (about 440M parameters) averaged nDCG@10 53.03 on their BEIR tasks, above monoT5 (3B) at 51.36 and above its own teacher (49.37).

scenes.caption: RankVicuna used the 100K-query RankGPT3.5 dataset from Sun et al.: each query's BM25 top 20 ranked by gpt-3.5-turbo.
About 12% of the teacher's permutations were malformed (bad format, missing ids, repeats) and were removed, so the student learns to always emit a clean ordering.

Training also includes shuffled input orders of the same candidates, to make the student robust to a poor initial ranking. RankZephyr adds random subsets of up to 20 passages so it handles variable window sizes.
The 7B student (Vicuna for RankVicuna; Zephyr-beta, built on Mistral, for RankZephyr) is fine-tuned on these permutations and served with the same sliding window as RankGPT.
RankZephyr adds a second stage: up to 5K queries ranked by RankGPT4 (generating it for all 100K was estimated at over USD 10K), and reaches or in some cases beats RankGPT4 as an open 7B model.

blocks.md: The pattern in production follows from all of this: a fast first stage, maybe a cross-encoder, then an LLM reranker on a short list, using either a distilled open model (RankZephyr-style listwise) or a capable API model with careful prompts, parsing and cost caps. Pointwise yes/no remains a strong cheap baseline when you have log-probabilities, and pairwise or setwise prompts are the choice when a smaller model must be robust to input order.

Pick the formulation by its failure mode: pointwise needs calibration, pairwise needs many calls, listwise needs a long context and a good initial order. Most practical gains come from controlling those failure modes (swapping, shuffling, cascades, distillation), not from a cleverer single prompt.

blocks.question: Your listwise reranker works well on BM25 input but degrades badly when you switch the first stage to a new retriever that returns candidates in a near-random order. Which fix targets the cause?
options: Increase the window step so fewer windows are needed
Lower the temperature to 0
Shuffle the input several times and aggregate the rankings, or use a student trained with shuffled inputs
Switch to query likelihood, which is order-free but needs no changes
blocks.explain: The symptom is order sensitivity: failures and the one-pass guarantee both lean on a good initial order. Permutation self-consistency marginalizes the order out, and RankVicuna/RankZephyr train on shuffled inputs for the same reason. Temperature 0 makes outputs repeatable, not order-invariant.

blocks.question: Why did RankGPT's distilled 440M DeBERTa reranker beat its ChatGPT teacher on BEIR?
options: It was trained on human relevance labels as well
It ranks each passage with a stable deterministic score instead of an occasionally malformed or inconsistent permutation
It used a longer context window than ChatGPT
It reranked 1000 passages instead of 100
blocks.explain: The student learns the teacher's preferences through a pairwise RankNet loss but scores each passage with a deterministic forward pass, so it avoids the teacher's missing ids, repetitions and window-to-window inconsistency. The authors attribute the gap to this stability.
